result: The manuscript provides background information on color-vision deficiencies (CVDs), including prevalence rates, genetic basis, and types of CVD. CVDs affect 2-8% of males and ~0.5% of females, with deuteranopia being the most common form affecting ~6% of males of European descent.
evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C21 provide well-established background knowledge about CVD prevalence, genetic basis, and phenotypes, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims establish the scientific context for the study.

result: Analysis of 66,253 images from eLife (2012-2022) revealed that 85.6% contained at least one color pair potentially problematic for deuteranopes, though only 2.6% were grayscale. Quantitative metrics showed bimodal distributions, with 7.3% of images having very low mean pixel-wise color distance (<0.01) between original and simulated versions.
evaluation: Claims C2, C22-C27 describe computational analysis of a large image dataset with clear quantitative results and statistical testing (Hartigans' Dip Test, p<0.001). The bimodal distribution finding is supported by appropriate statistical analysis, though the high percentage (85.6%) of potentially problematic images requires context from manual review to interpret meaningfully.

result: Manual review of 4,964 eLife images determined that 12.8% were 'Definitely problematic' for deuteranopes, while 77.9% were 'Definitely okay'. Spatial distances between colors and within-image labels frequently mitigated potential problems (54.2% and 48.4% of cases, respectively), even when problematic color pairs were present.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C28-C33 describe systematic manual review by two independent reviewers using defined criteria. The finding that spatial separation and labels mitigate problems is important and well-documented. However, the subjective nature of manual review and lack of inter-rater reliability metrics are limitations (acknowledged by authors in C60, C74-C75).

result: The percentage of 'Definitely problematic' articles in eLife declined significantly from 2012 to 2021 (p<0.001 by logistic regression), with a modest increase in 2022.
evaluation: Claims C5, C34-C35 report a temporal trend with appropriate statistical testing (logistic regression, p<0.001). The analysis properly accounts for pseudoreplication by categorizing at the article level. The finding suggests improving awareness over time, though the 2022 increase warrants caution in interpretation.

result: The frequency of problematic images differed significantly by subdiscipline (χ² test, p<0.001), with Cell Biology, Developmental Biology, and Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine having the highest percentages, while Evolutionary Biology, Genetics and Genomics, and Computational and Systems Biology had the lowest.
evaluation: Claims C6, C36-C38 report subdiscipline differences with appropriate statistical testing (χ² goodness-of-fit test, p<0.001). The pattern makes biological sense given the prevalence of fluorescence microscopy in cell-oriented disciplines. The analysis is properly conducted at the article level to avoid pseudoreplication.

result: Machine learning classification using five quantitative metrics showed that the number of high-ratio color pairs was the best single predictor (AUROC: 0.75; AUPRC: 0.34), while Logistic Regression combining all five metrics performed best among traditional algorithms (AUROC: 0.82; AUPRC: 0.43). All CNN configurations outperformed Logistic Regression.
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 describe systematic comparison of classification approaches using cross-validation. The performance metrics are clearly reported with appropriate measures (AUROC and AUPRC). The finding that CNNs outperform simpler methods is expected given the spatial nature of the problem, though the specific CNN configuration details in C42 are well-documented.

result: On the eLife hold-out test set (n=879), the CNN achieved AUROC of 0.89 and AUPRC of 0.77, substantially outperforming Logistic Regression (AUROC: 0.82, AUPRC: 0.49). Re-evaluation of 92 misclassified images revealed that 13 had been incorrectly labeled by reviewers, 31 had patterns that might confuse the model but labels were valid, and 48 had no identifiable confounding patterns.
evaluation: Claims C7, C43-C47 report hold-out test performance with appropriate metrics. The CNN shows strong performance (AUPRC 0.77 is good for an imbalanced problem). The post-hoc analysis of misclassifications (C45-C47) is valuable and suggests the model may sometimes be more accurate than human reviewers, though this finding should be interpreted cautiously.

result: On PubMed Central images (n=1,191), the CNN's performance dropped substantially (AUROC: 0.78, AUPRC: 0.39) compared to eLife. Only 5.2% of PubMed Central images were 'Definitely problematic' versus 12.8% for eLife, partly explained by the higher proportion of grayscale images in PubMed Central (38.5% vs 4.4%).
evaluation: Claims C8, C48-C53 document reduced model performance on an external dataset, which is honestly reported. The lower prevalence of problematic images in PubMed Central (5.2% vs 12.8%) and higher grayscale proportion provide context. However, the substantial performance drop (AUPRC from 0.77 to 0.39) indicates limited generalizability, which the authors acknowledge in C63-C66.

result: A web application was created at https://bioapps.byu.edu/colorblind_image_tester using Node.js and TensorFlow.js, implementing the Machado et al. 2009 deuteranopia simulation matrix (severity 0.8) and allowing users to upload images, view simulations, and obtain CNN predictions.
evaluation: Claims C9, C76-C78 describe the creation of a practical tool with clear technical specifications. The web application makes the research actionable for the scientific community. The implementation details are sufficiently documented for reproducibility.

result: Prior work on CVD simulation and image accessibility is reviewed, including simulation methods by Brettel et al., Viénot et al., and Machado et al., and accessibility studies by Frane (13.8% problematic in psychology journals) and Angerbauer et al. (60% accessible across CVD types, with slight improvement 2000-2019).
evaluation: Claims C54-C59 provide appropriate literature context with proper citations. The comparison to Frane's 13.8% finding validates the current study's 12.8% result. This background establishes the study's contribution within existing research.

result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: reliance on simulations rather than deuteranope experiences, use of a single severity threshold (0.8) that doesn't represent the full spectrum, imperfect mathematical color representations, focus only on deuteranopia, and substantial performance drop on PubMed Central likely due to dataset diversity and potential model bias toward eLife image patterns.
evaluation: Claims C60-C66 provide honest and thorough discussion of limitations. The authors appropriately acknowledge methodological constraints (simulation-based, single severity threshold) and model generalizability issues. These limitations are significant but do not invalidate the main findings, and the transparency is commendable.

result: The methodology involved downloading eLife images (June 1, 2022) from articles published 2012-2022 and PubMed Central images (March 21, 2024). Deuteranopia simulations used the colorspace package with severity 0.8, chosen to be stringent but reflecting moderate deuteranomaly rather than complete deuteranopia. Reviewers without deuteranopia performed manual review and did not define quantitative metrics to avoid confirmation bias.
evaluation: Claims C67-C75 document methodological details transparently. The choice of severity threshold (0.8) is explained and appropriate (C71-C72). The bias mitigation strategy (C75) is sound. The temporal scope is clearly defined, though the different download dates for eLife and PubMed Central (C67, C69) should be noted.
